statement: The Jesuit Reductions (semi-autonomous mission towns, established beginning c. 1609/1610 in the Paraná/Uruguay river basins) provided real, quantifiable protection from Portuguese bandeirante slave-raiding: between 1627-1640, an estimated 100,000 people were captured from the Guairá, Tape, and Itatín missions (~7,143/year); by 1632, roughly 12,000 Guarani had been forcibly displaced south and Guairá was effectively depopulated. Jesuits subsequently armed Guarani communities for self-defense; the Battle of Mbororé is recorded as the first decisive Guarani/Jesuit victory over Paulista slavers. Barbara Ganson, The Guaraní Under Spanish Rule in the Río de la Plata (Stanford University Press, 2003) — winner of the 2005 Murdo J. MacLeod Book Prize and a 2003 Choice Outstanding Academic Title — argues the Guarani were active agents shaping their own destiny under the mission system across the 16th-early 19th centuries, not passive victims of either colonialism or Jesuit paternalism. The popular film "The Mission" (1986) is documented (per dedicated academic film-history treatment) to romanticize Jesuit opposition to slavery generally — historically Jesuits raised limited or no objection to African slavery, and mission finances partly depended on estates using enslaved labor — and to compress over 100 years of mission history into roughly one dramatized year, largely omitting Guarani agency; the honest historical position sits between the film's romanticized "protective sanctuary" narrative and a flat "just another colonial imposition" reading.

sources.citation: Ganson, Barbara. The Guaraní Under Spanish Rule in the Río de la Plata. Stanford: Stanford University Press, 2003.
sources.author: Barbara Ganson

does_not_demonstrate: That the Jesuit Reductions were either a purely protective sanctuary (the romanticized popular-film reading) or a purely coercive colonial imposition with no real protective function or Guarani agency — Ganson's scholarship documents both real protection from slaving and real, ongoing Guarani agency within a genuinely constrained system
